introduction: On this third Sunday of Lent, God gives his people the Ten Words on Sinai, a law that begins with freedom: he is the God who brought them out of slavery. In the Gospel, Jesus drives the traders out of the temple and speaks of a new temple, his own body, which will be destroyed and raised in three days. Paul proclaims Christ crucified, the wisdom of God. Let us ask the Lord to cleanse the temple of our hearts.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Brothers and sisters, the law of the Lord is perfect and refreshes the soul. Let us turn to him in prayer.
intentions: For the Church, the temple built of living stones: that she may be a house of prayer for all peoples. Let us pray to the Lord.
For lawmakers and those who govern: that they may respect the dignity of every person and the good of families. Let us pray to the Lord.
For all who live under any kind of slavery or exploitation: that they may be set free and find people who stand beside them. Let us pray to the Lord.
For catechumens, and especially those who celebrate the scrutinies in these weeks: that Christ may free them from all that holds them back. Let us pray to the Lord.
For ourselves: that we may examine our lives in the light of the commandments and make a good confession before Easter. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: Lord God, you set your people free and gave them your law. Cleanse our hearts, make them a fit dwelling for your Spirit, and keep us faithful to your commandments. Through Christ our Lord.

reflection.title: Zeal for your house
reflection.body:
The Ten Commandments do not begin with a rule. They begin with a reminder: "I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage." God first sets his people free, and then shows them how to live as free people. The commandments are not a burden laid on slaves but a path for those who have been rescued. That is why the psalm can sing, "The LORD's law is perfect, restoring the soul."

In the Gospel, Jesus enters the temple at Passover and finds a market. He makes a whip of cords and drives out the animals and the money changers, saying, "Don't make my Father's house a marketplace!" His disciples remember a verse of the psalms: "Zeal for your house will eat me up."

When he is challenged, Jesus answers with a riddle: "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up." The crowd thinks of stones, but John explains: "But he spoke of the temple of his body." The place where God and humanity meet is now Jesus himself, crucified and risen.

Paul knows how strange this sounds. Some ask for signs and others for wisdom, "but we preach Christ crucified." To the world it looks like weakness, yet "the foolishness of God is wiser than men."

Lent is a good time to let Jesus into the temple of our own lives. What has turned our heart into a marketplace? Busyness, money worries, resentment, habits we no longer notice? This week, take the commandments slowly, one each day, as an examination of conscience. Then bring what you find to the sacrament of Reconciliation, and let the Lord cleanse his house.
